beats.script_body: Take the 4 or 5 train to Bowling Green, or the N/R to Whitehall Street. Begin from inside Bowling Green Park, standing at the bottom of Broadway and facing north — toward the bull. From here, it is remarkable to imagine that over the next twelve miles lies the longest avenue in America. But until the second quarter of the nineteenth century, New York City went no farther than City Hall, a fifteen-minute walk to the north.

beats.script_body: At Broadway's base lies Bowling Green Park, New York City's first official park, established in 1733. Its history runs to the business and leisure of the Dutch and English: it has been pasture for cows, parade ground for soldiers, and, true to its name, a bowling field for colonists. "Taxation and recreation," one might say, illustrates the park's varied history.

beats.script_body: By 1770, King George III was rewarded by the colonists with a gilded statue in the center of the park for his alleged efforts in repealing the Stamp Act; a year later the fence was added. In 1776, hours after the Declaration of Independence was read in what is now City Hall Park, enraged colonists and members of the Sons of Liberty beheaded the statue. Supposedly George's molten lead was then cast into musket balls later used to shoot Tory soldiers. The fence around Bowling Green is one of the oldest in the city; iron crowns adorned the gateposts until American revolutionaries sheared them off. Touch history — you can actually feel where this happened.

beats.script_body: Now home to the Museum of the American Indian and the U.S. Bankruptcy Court, this building was once the primary point for revenue collection in the United States. Before the income tax arrived in 1913, this was where the government made its money — and since New York was by far the leading port city in America, there was a huge amount of money to be made. As historian Henry Hope Reed once noted, if City Hall was run by the Democratic machine, the Custom House was certainly Republican. In fact it was Republican Chester Arthur who, as collector of customs of the Port of New York before becoming president on the death of James Garfield, set the wheels in motion for the building's construction.

beats.script_body: The 1907 Cass Gilbert masterpiece is a great example of New York City's beaux arts heritage. Beaux arts translates literally as "fine arts" and derives from the great French school, the École des Beaux Arts. But in the New York context the term takes on a larger meaning: it refers to buildings that evince civic pride, that express a grandeur and stateliness to match their civic function — whether that function be to house trains, books, or tax collectors.

beats.script_body: In front of the Custom House stand Daniel Chester French's limestone statues representing Asia, America, Europe, and Africa, from left to right — by the sculptor of the Lincoln Memorial. On the facade, Gilbert illustrates commerce: atop the cornice are twelve marble statues of history's most successful commercial states. Although you can't see it, the name Germany was effaced during World War I and replaced with Belgium. And gazing ahead from within every capital is Mercury, Roman god of commerce. Step into the museum to view the oval rotunda, decorated with a series of 1930s Works Progress Administration murals by Reginald Marsh.

beats.script_body: Look up Broadway at No. 26, on the corner of Broadway and Beaver, at the building topped with a cast-iron oil burner. The lantern expresses the building's function: it housed Standard Oil, John D. Rockefeller's monopolistic firm. But by the time this tower was built in 1924, the flame had long been extinguished — in 1911 the U.S. Supreme Court required the Standard Oil Holding Company to be dissolved and its directors to relinquish control of its subsidiaries. Standard Oil's offices remained here until the 1930s, when Rockefeller Center was constructed. And in 1796, the town residence of another financial giant, Alexander Hamilton, stood on this very site.

beats.script_body: Across the way, on the west side, 25 Broadway was the former central ticket office of the Cunard Shipping Line. Cunard, leader of the pack among the era's many steamship companies, put up this building in 1921 to house the firm that ran the fastest and most luxurious liners in the world. In the age of expensive cruises and mass immigration, this was big business — so much so that in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, this bottom stretch of Broadway was known as Steamship Row. Step inside (but not on Sunday) to see spectacular wall frescoes and maps outlining the old Cunard routes.

beats.script_body: Goldman Sachs, the notoriously secretive investment-banking concern, is housed in this creatively built octagonal structure at 85 Broad Street, which slices through Stone Street. The building was designed to conform to the irregular street pattern, and paving stones representing Stone Street actually cut right through Goldman Sachs's lobby. The partnership between Marcus Goldman and Samuel Sachs dates from 1882, when they joined forces to further the commercial-paper business Goldman had begun thirteen years earlier.

The tavern itself was run by an immigrant from the West Indies, Samuel Fraunces, who would soon become Washington's steward, and it was a popular watering hole of the day. It was also the site where the Committee of Correspondence — later the Continental Congress — held its first meeting.

beats.script_body: The building is a conjectural reproduction — no original bits survive save a few bricks — financed by the Sons of the Revolution in 1907. Its style is Georgian, named for those British kings and soon renamed "colonial" or "federal" in keeping with the antiroyalist mood of the new states. The block of Pearl Street just east represents one of the city's few remaining block-long groups of late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century shipping offices and warehouses; they were among the few that survived the Great Fire of 1835 unscathed. Thanks to the New York Landmarks Conservancy for saving them, the area is now the Fraunces Tavern Block Historic District.

beats.script_body: Here in Hanover Square sits lonely Abraham DePeyster — former mayor of New York City, colonial chief justice in the late seventeenth century, and prominent merchant — who once had a more princely view up Broadway when he stood in Bowling Green Park. The square was once the center of the city's publishing industry: William Bradford's New York Gazette, the city's first newspaper of 1725, had its printing offices here. It was also the home base of Captain Kidd, the privateer turned pirate. Tellingly, Hanover Square keeps the family name of the English kings — in sharp contrast to much of New York that changed its nomenclature after the Revolution.

beats.script_body: On the west side of the square is India House at One Hanover Square, built in the early 1850s. It was originally the Hanover Bank and later the New York Cotton Exchange, when cotton was king. Brownstone was once seen as unseemly for a proper home, but this building — like Trinity Church — helped change that, and in the later nineteenth century brownstone became a mark of dignity for New York's landed gentry. Today India House is one of Lower Manhattan's most exclusive business clubs; it takes its name from nautical trips to, and Orientalist fantasies of, the East, its original members more concerned with maritime issues than with banking.

beats.script_body: At 22 William, between Beaver and Exchange Place, is the City Bank Farmers' Trust Company Building of 1931. It has always been a curiosity in the canyons of Wall Street: it departs from the rectilinear and pivots as if ready to blast off, the irregular site pushing its architects to experiment. beats.script_body: The "Wall" in the name comes from an actual wall built by the Dutch. Governor Peter Stuyvesant had it erected in 1653, and it lasted until the latter seventeenth century, when colonists under British rule finally undermined it. Known in Dutch as De Wal, it was made of wooden planks stacked roughly nine feet high and was manned to keep both the British (until 1664) and the Indians away from New Amsterdam.

beats.script_body: At 55 Wall Street stands a building designed by Isaiah Rogers in 1842 to replace the Merchants Exchange, which had burned with seven hundred other buildings in the Great Fire of 1835. It served as the U.S. Custom House from 1863 to 1899 and later as a branch of Citibank. It's notable for a seamless arrangement of structure: the lower Ionic colonnade of 1842 — each column a single block of stone — works hand in glove with an upper Corinthian colonnade added seventy years later. The mammoth lobby measures 198 feet long and 132 feet high, and houses the largest display of Wedgewood china in the world around its central chandelier.

beats.script_body: At 40 Wall Street — originally the Bank of Manhattan — sits one of the great stories in American skyscraper construction. In the summer of 1929, longtime professional rivals and former partners William Van Alen and Craig Severance were hard at work trying to outdo each other in the battle for dominant skyscraper height. The Woolworth Tower still held sway as the city's tallest, but Severance was convinced to the last moment that his Bank of Manhattan would outdo Van Alen's automotive giant, the Chrysler Building, and dethrone Frank Woolworth. Hidden from view, and unveiled only at the final moment of the competition, was Chrysler's razor-sharp spire — its additional 125 feet outdid 40 Wall and brought the Chrysler Building the fame of being the tallest. Severance's consolation prize? 40 Wall broke all records for speed, finished in eleven months with over a million square feet of floor space. For Van Alen, success was short-lived: the Empire State unseated the Chrysler after only eighteen months. As for the Bank of Manhattan, in five years it dropped to fifth-tallest in the country — today it's at number 30 and counting.

beats.script_body: Built like a fortress in 1924, the Federal Reserve Bank was made to resist the elements. It is not New York snobbery to call it the most significant of the thirteen Federal Reserve sites. Its limestone facade is noted for weathering in different tones — notice how they change from light to dark — and the magnificent wrought-iron lanterns were designed by the Philadelphian Samuel Yellin. The Federal Reserve itself was set up in 1914 to have a central bank, rather than one person, make policy: in 1907, for example, J. P. Morgan personally mobilized enough banking support to stave off a collapse that could have rivaled the Great Depression.

beats.script_body: Westward at 14 Wall stands the Bankers Trust Building. Bankers Trust is no more, but Trowbridge and Livingston's pyramidal top — modeled on antiquity's mausoleum at Halicarnassus — remains one of the great pinnacles in a city bathed in sumptuous finishing touches. J. P. Morgan even shacked up beneath the pyramid to have a bird's-eye view of the construction of his own building across the street. The pyramid became the logo of Bankers Trust for years, though, in a testimony to the downtown canyons, you cannot see it from Wall Street itself. Inside, peek at the bronze lobby gates representing the enterprises of capitalism — metallurgy, shipping, mining, agriculture, and power.

beats.script_body: On the northeast corner of Nassau and Wall stands Federal Hall National Memorial, dubbed the "Parthenon of Wall Street." The site has a vigorous past as the city's second city hall, later the Custom House and subtreasury, and now a federal museum. The current Greek-revival structure dates from 1842; the earlier building on the site, where Washington took his oath and the new government operated for its first eighteen months, was designed by Pierre L'Enfant — the master planner of Washington, D.C. — and was demolished in 1790 when the capital moved to Philadelphia. The Greek-revival style suited an age when Athenian democracy and the Greek independence movement produced a bumper crop of Doric-templed civic buildings; later, as abolitionism gained steam, Greece became associated with slavery rather than the demos, and those classical buildings lost their place in the sun.

beats.script_body: The forlorn little tree out front on Broad Street isn't any old tree but a buttonwood, or sycamore. In 1792, twenty-four brokers met under a buttonwood — in actuality further east on Wall Street — and began trading the massive debt from the Revolutionary War. The so-called Buttonwood Agreement, as Edwin Burrows and Michael Wallace tell us in Gotham, "laid the foundations for a structured securities market." Early the next year the traders moved into the Tontine Coffee House on the northwest corner of Water and Wall — a site that had been the locale for the infamous Royal African Trading Company, where the English bought and sold enslaved Africans.

beats.script_body: Directly across Broad Street from Morgan's building is the sine qua non of capitalist institutions, the New York Stock Exchange — even if its address is on Broad Street, it's the best known of Wall Street's buildings. beats.script_body: New York City was no stranger to slavery: it was the largest slaveholding city in all the colonies until 1750, and the number-one place for slave importation and auctions. Slaves arrived as early as 1626 from the Dutch West Indies, but on September 15, 1655, the Witte Paert docked with three hundred African slaves, signaling the city's beginning as a large-scale port for the transatlantic slave trade. By 1664 the city was 20 to 25 percent black. Under the Dutch, some were given "half freedom" — a degree of freedom in housing and employment, though even half-free blacks had to work for the Dutch West India Company when needed, and their children were company property. When the British conquered in 1664 they recognized all slave property, eliminated half-free status, and made freedom harder each year; in 1706 a law decreed that conversion to Christianity did not affect a slave's status. New York City held 3,137 slaves by 1771. The institution was dismantled only gradually: the Manumission Society began work in 1785, the Gradual Manumission Act of 1799 freed males born after that year at twenty-eight and females at twenty-five, and full emancipation finally took effect in 1827.

The Gradual Manumission Act of 1799 freed males born after that year at age twenty-eight and females at age twenty-five... legislation emancipating all slaves finally took effect in 1827.

beats.script_body: New York saw several significant slave uprisings in the eighteenth century, most notably the 1712 uprising on Maiden Lane and Nassau Street — the present site of the Home Insurance Company. There more than fifty armed slaves gathered for an uprising that killed nine white settlers before the slaves dispersed to the north. Ultimately nineteen participants were captured and executed in gruesome fashion — by hanging, burning, and goring — to intimidate the remaining slave population.

beats.script_body: The building at 1 Wall Street now houses the Bank of New York, which absorbed the original owners, Irving Trust, in 1988 — at the time the building carried the highest real-estate price tag of any site in New York City. Inside, the three-story reception hall is one of the most glorious interiors in Manhattan: this is Art Deco at its most majestic, soaring and emboldened. Lewis Mumford called 1 Wall Street a building of "untrammeled imagination." At the very top of the fluted skyscraper sits a gilded mosaic boardroom, testament to the extravagance of a different age — before the golden age of Deco came to a screeching halt with the Great Depression.

beats.script_body: There was a time when churches were all one could see on the skyline, and Trinity, at 280 feet, was the highest point in New York City until surpassed by the towers of the Brooklyn Bridge — which says a lot about commerce. Trinity began as a land grant from King William III to the colonists in the late seventeenth century; the church originally controlled all the land from Fulton up to Christopher Street. Many early belfrymen, pastors, and rectors now have city streets named after them — Chambers, Murray, and Reade, for example. Trinity has gone through three incarnations: the first (1698-1776) burned in the fire of 1776, the second saw its roof implode in 1839, and the present building by Richard Upjohn has withstood the ravages of time.

beats.script_body: Walk the churchyard and you'll meet an illustrious gathering of the city's financial elite and early purveyors of freedom. Alexander Hamilton was buried here after his fateful duel with Vice President Aaron Burr in Weehawken; Robert Fulton, inventor of the steamship, is memorialized; William Bradford, publisher of New York's first newspaper, rests here; and so does Francis Lewis, the only signer of the Declaration of Independence buried in Manhattan. Opposite Pine Street stands the Soldiers/Martyrs monument, erected in 1852 to soldiers who died imprisoned in the Rhinelander Sugar House during the Revolution — of the war's 18,500 who died in captivity, more than half perished in New York.

beats.script_body: Take a detour through the graveyard and down the stairs to Trinity Place to peek at the American Stock Exchange. The AMEX has its roots at the curbstone of Broad Street and Exchange Place, where "curb brokers" would literally stop at nothing to buy and sell. Only in 1921 — after fifty-six years — did the New York curb market find a home, and in 1953 it was officially designated the American Stock Exchange.

beats.script_body: Standing on Thames Street opposite 120 Broadway gives a crash course in New York City's first zoning ordinance. The Equitable Building's extreme mass — floor area thirty times the site's area, shafts going straight up forty floors, forty-five acres of floor space on a site just over an acre — was discouraging enough that light and air became the most desired commodities on the block. The new ordinance called for a "zoning envelope" that forced what became known as the "setback": the stepped-back, stairlike recesses you see as buildings grow taller. Spurred on by Hugh Ferris's exquisite drawings, setbacks became a design challenge, each architect trying to outdo the next in geometry and flair.

beats.script_body: You may wonder how, in this dense and overoccupied district, an open-air plaza with benches managed to emerge here at Liberty Plaza. It was the great Seagram Building on Park Avenue, with its pristine plaza and open space, that convinced the city to find incentives for developers to allow more public use. Thus was born the 1961 zoning ordinance, which rewarded builders who provided public space integrated with private buildings.

beats.script_body: Directly west of Liberty Plaza once stood the seven-building complex of the World Trade Center, spotlighted by the twin towers — Towers 1 and 2 — the third-tallest buildings in the world. In the greatest act of terror to occur on American soil, almost three thousand persons lost their lives on September 11, 2001, when two hijacked planes were crashed into the towers, resulting in horrible fires and the buildings' implosion. As the authors wrote, it was too early to know what would become of this tragic space — but in New York's unceasing effort to rebuild that which is torn down, it was unlikely the area would remain fallow far into the future. The question of how to memorialize echoed the long-debated African burial ground just north near City Hall.

beats.script_body: Across Broadway, the Marine Midland Bank Building at 140 Broadway shows what an ambitious developer could do. It was uncommon — impossible, really — in the late 1960s and 1970s for a developer to think about quality as a way of attracting tenants, but Harry Helmsley was ahead of his time. He hired one of the great international-style architects, Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore Owings and Merrill, who also designed the Chase building behind it, as well as the sculptor Isamu Noguchi. The result is a sleek, refined glass exterior, and Noguchi's contribution is an orange cube — to be exact, a six-sided rhombohedron — with a cut-out hole.

Helmsley was moved to hire one of the great international style architects, Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore Owings and Merrill (who also designed the Chase Manhattan building behind it in 1960), as well as the sculptor Isamu Noguchi... The result is a sleek, refined, glass exterior that adds dignity to this stretch of Broadway. Noguchi's moving contribution is an orange cube (well, to be exact, it's a rhombohedron—a six-sided figure) with a cut-out hole.

beats.script_body: On the site of today's U.S. Steel Building at 1 Liberty Plaza once stood one of the great downtown buildings, the Singer Building. Perhaps the mourning wasn't as great as when Pennsylvania Station was slaughtered in 1963, but the Singer Building's demolition brought tears of rage consistent with its long-standing place in the skyline. Its tragic epitaph: it is the tallest building ever to be demolished.

beats.script_body: The tallest building in the world from 1913 to 1929, the Woolworth at 233 Broadway is symbolized by its trademarked name, the "Cathedral of Commerce." It was Frank Woolworth's revolutionary genius to open stores where the buyer could touch, feel, and examine every item — and it made him a mint. The exterior is dressed in late Gothic style, its terra-cotta facade and clear base-shaft-tower form making it, for many enthusiasts, the archetype of a skyscraper. Inside, look for the magnificent gargoyles, including Cass Gilbert the architect and Woolworth himself counting the nickels and dimes with which he literally paid for the building — in full, with $13 million in cash, so it never had a mortgage.

The exterior of the building is dressed up in late Gothic style... specifically the terra cotta used throughout the facade; the clear and articulated form of the base, shaft, and tower... you have time to appreciate several magnificent gargoyles, including Cass Gilbert (the architect) and Woolworth himself counting the nickels and dimes with which he (literally) paid for the building.
